name: Bolandione
lead: Bolandione, also called 19-norandrostenedione, is a steroid that the body converts into nandrolone, an anabolic steroid. It was sold in the United States as an over-the-counter prohormone supplement until 2005, and bodybuilders and gym users took it as a way to raise anabolic hormone levels in pursuit of more muscle mass and a fuller physique [1][2].

The idea behind prohormones is that they act as a one-step precursor: after oral dosing, bolandione is converted to nandrolone, which supporters expected to add muscle and strength and help reduce body fat [1][2]. Supplement makers marketed such products on those claims. A 2003 review of androstenedione-related prohormones concluded that most human studies did not support the marketed claims and raised concerns about estrogen levels and blood lipids with long-term oral use [2].

Bolandione is now a US Schedule III controlled substance and is prohibited under the World Anti-Doping Code [1]. It is also a notable name in anti-doping science, because trace amounts in over-the-counter androstenedione products produced positive tests for a nandrolone metabolite [3].

chain: Oral prohormone converted to nandrolone in the body
Claimed gains in muscle and leaner physique
angle.text: Users took bolandione supplements expecting it to convert to nandrolone and build muscle for a larger, leaner physique. The human studies reviewed for androstenedione-type prohormones did not support the marketed muscle claims.

paras: In the late 1990s and early 2000s, bolandione was part of the andro prohormone supplement category, sold alongside androstenedione and androstenediols and marketed to the general public for strength, muscle mass, fat loss, mood and sexual performance [2]. Products sold under names such as D-Bol combined 19-norandrostenedione with 4-androstenediol, according to a T Nation poster describing a teenager's supplements [4].
Users in the T Nation community discussed andro products in the context of the 2004 US bill to control them, and later in discussions of whether the prohormone ban could be overturned [5][6].

Wikipedia reports that bolandione is readily converted to nandrolone after oral dosing, though it activates the androgen receptor about ten times less potently than DHT [1]. A 2009 animal study described oral dosing as a very ineffective way to build skeletal muscle, and a 2008 rat study found muscle-selective effects with weak androgenic activity when given subcutaneously [1].
19-norandrostenedione is also produced in small amounts in the body and has been proposed to be a minor by-product of aromatization of androgens [7].

A 2000 randomized trial of 41 men found that trace contamination of over-the-counter androstenedione products with 19-norandrostenedione could produce urine tests positive for the nandrolone metabolite 19-norandrosterone, and that administration of 19-norandrostenedione itself did so [3]. A 2010 study found that a supplement matrix such as an energy bar changed peak urinary 19-norandrosterone after a trace dose [8].
Studies also show the same metabolite can arise from the progestogen norethisterone, which can contain 19-norandrostenedione as an impurity [9].

A 2003 review of oral andro prohormone supplementation reported elevated estrogen-related hormones, declines in HDL cholesterol and increased cardiovascular risk markers in several studies, and said the research base raised concerns about long-term use [2].

Bolandione was sold over the counter in the US until 2005 [1]. The Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2004 was introduced in the US House to extend controls to such products [5]. It is a Schedule III substance and a banned doping agent [1].

No studies found testing bolandione for muscle or appearance outcomes in humans. Human research involves doping-control trials on urinary metabolites [3][8] and reviews of the wider andro prohormone category [2].

timeline.event: JAMA study shows contaminated androstenedione supplements can cause positive nandrolone metabolite tests.[3]
Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2004 introduced in the US House.[5]
Over-the-counter sales end in the US.[1]

claims.believers: Users and sellers of 19-nor products such as D-Bol-type stacks expected oral conversion to produce anabolic effects [4].
claims.experts: A 2003 review found most studies contradicted marketing claims for andro prohormones and flagged estrogen and cholesterol effects [2]. Wikipedia cites animal work describing oral dosing as very ineffective for muscle [1].

card.summary: A nandrolone prohormone from the supplement era; now controlled and best known for causing doping-test positives.
card.note: US Schedule III; banned in sport.

quick.overview:
Bolandione is a prohormone that the body converts to nandrolone. It was sold as a supplement in the US until 2005.

It is now a controlled substance and is chiefly remembered for doping-test false positives.
quick.mechanism: Oral intake leads to conversion to nandrolone; its own androgen receptor activity is weaker than DHT.
quick.risks: US Schedule III and prohibited in sport. Animal data suggest oral routes are inefficient for muscle but may still cause side effects, per Wikipedia.
